clue.text: Theoretical only, like Auden's graffiti?

definitions.meaning: of purely scholarly interest, with no practical bearing
W. H. Auden published a book of clerihews called ... Graffiti

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses Auden's scribblings as of no practical use.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means scholarly with no practical application, and it is also the adjective in the title of Auden's light-verse collection.

clue.text: Down Two Gentlemen of Verona

parts.note: not Shakespeare's comedy of that name but the two feuding Veronese heads of household in Romeo and Juliet, whose surnames fill this light and 6 down

explanation.surface: The title of Shakespeare's early comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' is the heading of the clue list caught by the scan. The title points at The Two Gentlemen of Verona, but the two men meant are old Capulet and old Montague from Romeo and Juliet; this light takes the first family name, 6 down the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Juliet's father, head of one of Verona's two warring noble houses, is one of the gentlemen of that city.

clue.text: "As Lord —— says, "there are thome thingth no fellow can underthtand'" (Lucy Maud Montgomery, Anne of the Island)

definitions.text: "As Lord —— says, "there are thome thingth no fellow can underthtand'" (Lucy Maud Montgomery, Anne of the Island)

parts.words: "As Lord —— says, "there are thome thingth no fellow can underthtand'" (Lucy Maud Montgomery, Anne of the Island)
parts.note: the missing name is the lisping foppish lord of Tom Taylor's play Our American Cousin, whose catchphrase Montgomery quotes

explanation.surface: A line from Anne of the Island quoting a lisping stage aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The lisp ('thome thingth') is the clue: Lord Dundreary of Our American Cousin spoke like this, and his long side-whiskers gave 'dundrearies' their name.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted lord is the comic peer from Taylor's 1858 play, famous for his lisp and catchphrase.

clue.text: Unassuming proposal by Swift

definitions.meaning: Jonathan Swift's 1729 satire is A ... Proposal

explanation.surface: Swift's suggestion sounds humble enough.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift's 'proposal' was that the Irish poor sell their children as food, so the adjective in his title is ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means humble, and it is the word qualifying the proposal in the title of Swift's satire.

clue.text: Possibly islander, present at the passing of James Cook in Dickens story

definitions.text: Possibly islander, present at the passing of James Cook
definitions.meaning: Captain James Cook was killed by Hawaiian islanders in 1779, so one of them could be called the killer of the captain
one of the Nurse's Stories told in Dickens's The Uncommercial Traveller is about a Bluebeard figure of this name

explanation.surface: A Hawaiian at Cook's death turns up in a tale by Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part literally: whoever killed Captain Cook was a murderer of a captain. 'in' links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who killed Captain Cook killed a ship's commander, and the same two words name the wife-killing villain of Dickens's nursery tale.

clue.text: A scrum arranged by Brutus?

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are set out in a new order, as players are arranged in a scrum

explanation.surface: Brutus organises a rugby scrum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges A SCRUM. The question mark marks the definition as an example: Brutus is the cognomen of Marcus Junius Brutus.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's and history's Brutus had the first name Marcus, so Brutus is one bearer of it.

clue.text: See 2

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'See 2': the light is the second half of the 2-down answer pair (the two Verona families), but the puzzle file carries no group linking it to 2-down, so it has no clue of its own to annotate

clue.text: Archangelic musician, no relation to Marie

definitions.text: Archangelic musician, no relation to Marie

parts.words: Archangelic musician, no relation to Marie
parts.note: the Baroque violinist-composer whose first name was Arcangelo shares a surname with the Victorian novelist Marie, though they were unrelated

explanation.surface: A heavenly musician is no kin to a woman named Marie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archangelic' plays on Arcangelo, the composer's first name; Marie Corelli was the pen name of the novelist Mary Mackay, so there is truly no relation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian Baroque composer Arcangelo shares his surname with the pen name of the novelist Marie, who was no kin.

clue.text: Distress signal he sent codified, for Macedonian general

parts.note: SOS is the Morse distress signal

indicators.note: put into a code, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

explanation.surface: A man in trouble sends a coded SOS for a general from Macedon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'codified' is the anagram signal on 'he sent'. Sosthenes held power in Macedon in 279 BC, during the Gallic invasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Sosthenes briefly ruled Macedon as a general in 279 BC, fighting off the invading Gauls.

clue.text: Began like frank journalist

parts.note: frank and open both mean candid
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A candid reporter started out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like' is a link word: a frank editor is an OPEN ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To have opened something is to have started it.

clue.text: Homeric archer in mishap, and a rush to hospital

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Homeric archer in mishap, and a rush to hospital': AND A RUSH rearranged gives ANDARUSH, with H where the answer needs P, and no word supplies P or removes H, so the clue as held is garbled or misread
annotationWithheld.clue: Homeric archer in mishap, and a rush to hospital

clue.text: "The affair is over, — lives " wrote Lovelace

definitions.text: "The affair is over, — lives " wrote Lovelace

parts.words: "The affair is over, — lives " wrote Lovelace
parts.note: the rake Lovelace writes this line in Samuel Richardson's epistolary novel, naming its heroine, whom he has just wronged

explanation.surface: A quotation from a letter by a cavalier named Lovelace.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace is not the poet Richard Lovelace but the seducer in Richardson's novel, whose letter reads 'And now, Belford, I can go no farther. The affair is over. Clarissa lives.'
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Richardson's novel is the woman Lovelace writes of after his crime.

clue.text: Stowe's dandy creation

parts.note: in Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin, St. Clare's vain, overdressed valet is a dandy

explanation.surface: Harriet Beecher Stowe invented a fine character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dandy' looks like slang for excellent, but it describes the character: a foppish servant who wears his master's clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The foppish valet of Augustine St. Clare in Uncle Tom's Cabin bears this name.

clue.text: Exodus campsite in Dorset hamlet

indicators.note: the place sits inside the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Israelites pitch camp in a Dorset village.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'DorsET HAMlet'. Etham is where the Israelites camped 'in the edge of the wilderness' (Exodus 13:20).
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Exodus names this place as the Israelites' second encampment after leaving Egypt.

clue.text: Productions of one of our most precious writers

definitions.text: Productions of one of our most precious writers

parts.words: Productions of one of our most precious writers
parts.note: John Lyly's prose romance Euphues gave its name to an ornate, mannered prose style, and 'precious' means affected rather than valuable

explanation.surface: Works by a highly valued English author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precious' suggests treasured, but here means over-refined: the elaborate antithesis and alliteration of Lyly's Euphues.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaborate turns of style in the manner of Lyly's Euphues are what such a mannered writer produces.

clue.text: Our superiors are guided by it, Addison thought, and our inferiors by instinct

definitions.text: Our superiors are guided by it, Addison thought, and our inferiors by instinct

parts.words: Our superiors are guided by it, Addison thought, and our inferiors by instinct
parts.note: Joseph Addison in The Spectator ranked creatures with angels guided by immediate knowing above humans, and beasts by instinct below

explanation.surface: Addison's remark on how higher and lower beings are led.
explanation.walkthrough: Addison's point is that reason sits between direct insight (for angels) and instinct (for animals).
explanation.definitionFit: Immediate understanding without reasoning is what Addison credited to beings above humans.

clue.text: So tribune somehow gets to be Roman general

indicators.note: in some way or other, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tribune somehow rises to command a Roman army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges SO TRIBUNE. Gaius Trebonius was a general under Caesar and one of his assassins.
explanation.definitionFit: Trebonius commanded legions for Caesar in Gaul before joining the conspiracy against him.

clue.text: Well-known slapstick writer

parts.note: Kurt ... wrote the 1976 novel Slapstick, so he is a writer of that book rather than of knockabout comedy

explanation.surface: A famous author of pratfall comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slapstick' reads as a genre, but it is the title of a Vonnegut novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist wrote Slapstick, or Lonesome No More!, which makes him its author.

clue.text: "What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba?" (mother and son)

definitions.text: "What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba?" (mother and son)

parts.words: "What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba?" (mother and son)
parts.note: Hamlet's question gets a literal answer: Hecuba was the mother of the youngest son of Priam, murdered by Polymestor

explanation.surface: Hamlet's line about the player weeping for Hecuba.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's question is rhetorical, but the bracket answers it: the 'him' who is son to Hecuba is the son whose ghost opens Euripides' Hecuba.
explanation.definitionFit: Priam and Hecuba's youngest son, sent to Thrace for safety and killed there, is the son the bracket asks for.

clue.text: Siren as preferred blonde

definitions.meaning: a seductive female spirit luring sailors to wreck, as on the Rhine rock
Anita Loos's novel Gentlemen Prefer Blondes has the gold-digger heroine ... Lee

explanation.surface: A seductress, as the blonde gentlemen prefer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'preferred blonde' points to the title Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, whose heroine shares her first name with the Rhine siren.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine maiden who lured boatmen is a siren, and Loos's blonde heroine has the same first name.

clue.text: They supply all the action in the story

definitions.text: They supply all the action in the story

parts.words: They supply all the action in the story
parts.note: read grammatically, the words that express actions in a narrative are the doing words

explanation.surface: Characters who drive the plot of a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests characters or events; the grammatical reading is the doing words of the text.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar calls the parts of speech that express action doing words.

clue.text: Alicia Meadowes's daring was sweet

parts.note: Alicia Meadowes wrote the Regency romance Sweet ..., so her daring was sweet by title

explanation.surface: A romance writer's boldness was charming.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reverses the title Sweet Bravado: the noun meaning daring follows 'Sweet' in the novel's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A show of boldness is daring, and Meadowes paired the word with 'Sweet' in a novel title.

clue.text: Rip off Jason's trophy

definitions.meaning: Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis to win the Golden one

explanation.surface: Someone tears away the prize Jason won.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means swindle, and the noun is the golden ram's coat Jason carried off.

clue.text: Finish, say, sort of tongue

parts.note: Finnish, spelt here as the word for ending, belongs to the Finno-Ugric family of languages

explanation.surface: A command to stop talking, as in 'hold your tongue'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish' looks like a verb but stands for the language of Finland, an example of the family, hence 'say'.
explanation.definitionFit: Finnish and Hungarian belong to the Ugric or Finno-Ugric family of languages.

clue.text: Let in 24 hours to Woolf character

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other

explanation.surface: Letting out a room for a day to a Woolf heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal. '24 hours' looks like a cross-reference to another light, but here it simply means a day.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa, of Woolf's novel Mrs Dalloway, has this married surname.

clue.text: Author spotted in rehearsal in Germany

indicators.note: the author is seen sitting inside the run of letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A writer was seen at a rehearsal in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across 'rehearSAL IN GERmany'.
explanation.definitionFit: J. D. Salinger wrote The Catcher in the Rye.

clue.text: He foresaw hostilities between Israel and Syria

definitions.text: He foresaw hostilities between Israel and Syria

parts.words: He foresaw hostilities between Israel and Syria
parts.note: a biblical prophet of the northern kingdom, in the time of Ahab, who in 1 Kings is sent to anoint Hazael king of Syria, Israel's coming enemy

explanation.surface: A pundit predicting war in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as modern commentary; the man meant is the Old Testament prophet who anointed Hazael, later scourge of Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tishbite prophet of 1 Kings was told to anoint Hazael, the Syrian king who would war on Israel.

clue.text: Instrument gives back time

explanation.surface: A musical instrument returns the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives back' suggests a reversal, but 'back' is SPINE and 'gives' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A small harpsichord with one string per note is a keyboard instrument.

clue.text: Sort of postered set of organ pipes

indicators.note: sort is taken as a verb, to arrange, so the letters of the next word are reordered

explanation.surface: A rank of organ pipes plastered with posters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like 'kind of', but is the anagram signal working on POSTERED.
explanation.definitionFit: A stop of reed pipes, sounded by a vibrating tongue, is a set of pipes on an organ.
